answer: A sharp sportsbook is one that prices with low margin, accepts large bets, and keeps taking action from bettors who win, using them to sharpen its lines instead of banning them. In 2026 the list is short: Pinnacle (outside the US), Circa (a few US states), the betting exchanges Betfair, Matchbook and Smarkets (outside the US), and the US exchanges and prediction markets (Kalshi, Polymarket US, Novig, ProphetX, Sporttrade) where there is no house margin at all. Everything else limits winners.

blocks.p: The economics explain the behavior. A retail book makes money from the margin and from recreational losses, so a customer who beats the margin is a cost. A sharp book makes money from volume at a thin margin and uses the sharpest customers as free information about where the line should be. An exchange or prediction market makes money from commission on both sides and does not care who wins.

The standard against which every other book is measured. Pinnacle posts markets with roughly 2% margin, raises limits as the game approaches, and publishes a winners-welcome policy. Its closing line is the usual benchmark for closing line value. Not available to US residents.

The closest thing to Pinnacle inside the US. Circa prices its own numbers, takes large NFL bets in Nevada and its other states, and does not limit on skill. Its market list is narrower than a retail book's and its app is plainer; its customers do not care.

blocks.h3: Bookmaker, BetCRIS, and the offshore sharp books

blocks.p: Several offshore books have long-standing reputations for taking sharp action. They are not licensed in the US and are outside this list's scope; a US bettor's regulated options for sharp pricing are Circa and the exchanges.

sections.h2: Why exchanges and prediction markets belong on this list

blocks.p: By the definition above, an exchange is the sharpest book possible: zero margin, limits set only by liquidity, and no concept of limiting a winner. Betfair's closing prices on soccer are at least as sharp as Pinnacle's. In the US, Kalshi and Polymarket US have built sports books deep enough that their closing prices on NFL and NBA games are a credible benchmark, and Novig and ProphetX bring the same mechanics to sports-only exchanges. For an American bettor in 2026, "sharp sportsbooks" mostly means these.

sections.h2: Books that are often called sharp but are not

list: Reduced-juice retail books. A -105 line is a good price, but if the book limits you after a winning month it is a promotion, not a policy.
Books with high limits for public bets only. Large limits on primetime favorites and small limits on derivatives is retail behavior with a bigger number on the front.
Market-making books that copy Pinnacle. Copying a sharp line is not the same as being sharp; the tell is what happens to your account when you beat it.

sections.h2: Using sharp books without an account at each one

blocks.p: The practical problem with the list is that the sharpest price moves between its members through the day, and a bettor who wants it needs balances at all of them. Pinnacle and the big exchanges are closed to US residents, Circa is in a handful of states, and the prediction markets and US exchanges each have their own app, balance and fee schedule. Consolidating that into one place is the job of a cross-venue terminal.

takeaways: Sharp books price at about 2% margin, take large bets and keep taking action from winners.
Pinnacle and Circa are the sharp sportsbooks; Betfair, Matchbook and Smarkets are the sharp exchanges abroad.

faq.a: Pinnacle, by reputation and by margin, outside the US. Inside the US, Circa among sportsbooks, and the deep exchanges and prediction markets where there is no margin at all.

faq.q: Is Pinnacle available in the US?
faq.a: No. Pinnacle does not accept US residents.

faq.q: Which US sportsbooks do not limit winners?
faq.a: Circa Sports, in its states. Outside sportsbooks proper, the exchanges and prediction markets (Kalshi, Polymarket US, Novig, ProphetX, Sporttrade) do not limit because they have no exposure to your result.

faq.q: Is a betting exchange a sharp sportsbook?
faq.a: By every measure that defines sharpness, yes: no margin, high effective limits on liquid markets, and no account restrictions. It is not technically a bookmaker.

faq.q: What margin does a sharp book charge?
faq.a: Roughly 2% on major sides and totals (-104 to -106 each side), rising on props and smaller markets. Retail books charge about 4.8% on the same markets.
No. Their price is the offer. Bonuses are funded by margin, and a sharp book has little of it to spend.
